title: Five loaves and two fish (John 6:1–14)
hook: a boy hands over his lunch and five thousand are fed
carry: what you hand over is enough

segments.voice: Last week ended with the workers hired late, each paid the same denarius: grace isn't a wage. Now a new week: signs on the road. And it starts with a lunch.
screen: `GRACE ISN'T A WAGE.` → `WEEK EIGHT: SIGNS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: A hillside by the Sea of Galilee, near Passover, with much grass in the place, John says. A huge crowd has followed Jesus out here, thousands of people, a long way from any town. It's getting late. Everybody's hungry. Jesus turns to Philip, one of his disciples, and asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?" John adds that he asked this to test him, because he already knew what he would do. Philip counts the cost. Two hundred pence worth of bread, he says, wouldn't be enough for each of them to get a little. The need is enormous, and what they've got is nothing.
screen: `A HILLSIDE, A HUGE CROWD.` → `WHERE WILL WE BUY BREAD?` → `PHILIP COUNTS THE COST.`

segments.voice: Then Andrew speaks up, honest and a little embarrassed: "There is a boy here that hath five barley loaves, and two fishes; but what are these among so many?" John is the one who tells us it was a boy, and that the loaves were barley. Some readers note that barley bread was plain, everyday bread. This is a kid's packed lunch, and not a fancy one. Jesus says: make the people sit down. There's a lot of grass there, and the men sit down, about five thousand of them. Then Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. The Greek word for gave thanks is the root of a word Catholics know well: Eucharist. John's chapter six goes on, the next day, to Jesus calling himself the bread of life, and the Church reads this hillside meal as pointing toward the Mass. Then a detail that's easy to miss. When everyone's full, Jesus says: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Nothing wasted, and more left over than they started with. In John's telling, it starts with a child who handed over what he had, even though everyone could see it wasn't enough.
screen: `FIVE BARLEY LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `A BOY'S PLAIN LUNCH.` · `HE GAVE THANKS — EUCHARIST.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.` · then, large: `BUT WHAT ARE THESE AMONG SO MANY?`

segments.voice: Think of a need that seems too big, a friend's grief, a neighbor's struggle, a cause you care about, and of what you actually have. Not much: ten minutes, twenty dollars, one skill, a listening ear, five loaves and two fish. Choose one small thing you think won't matter and picture handing it over anyway; if you pray, you can offer it to God and let him do the rest.
Eucharist. The thanksgiving behind a boy's five loaves and two fish, feeding thousands with baskets of bread left over.
Your line: what you hand over is enough. Twelve baskets, from one small lunch. Day fifty, done.

howItsDone: Catholics read John 6 over several summer Sundays in the year of Mark, from the feeding on the hillside through the bread of life discourse, and hear it as pointing to the Eucharist.

chat.says: How did Jesus feed five thousand people? Where did the food come from?
options: A boy's five barley loaves and two fish; Jesus gave thanks and shared them.
The disciples bought bread with two hundred pence from a nearby town.
Rich followers had brought a cart of bread and fish there in advance.
chat.meaning: Andrew found a boy with five barley loaves and two fishes. Jesus gave thanks, handed them out, and twelve baskets were left over.

Passover.meaning: the spring feast of the Jewish people

barley.meaning: a grain for plain, everyday bread

pence.meaning: old English coins, the Douay-Rheims's word

Eucharist.meaning: from the Greek for giving thanks; the Mass's holy meal

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 6:5, 6:9, 6:12 given from memory; confirm.
'Not counting women and children' comes from Matthew 14:21, not John; the script folds it in. Confirm or remove.
Two hundred denarii (6:7) rendered as 'two hundred days' wages'; confirm.
Barley bread as the bread of the poor: standard background; confirm.
'The only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell': commonly stated; confirm.
John 6 read on Sundays 17–21 of Ordinary Time in Year B; confirm.
